j.learned_fact: Diwali is celebrated by lighting lamps/candles, and more lit candles make a room brighter. The claim 'we light five candles because five is our special number' is not a real Diwali custom (Diwali lasts five days; lamp counts vary) and reads as invented.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (more candles, more light)
j.notes: The cultural content is vague and partly invented, and the shopkeeper who 'touched his ear, showing he listened with joy' is a nonsensical detail that a 4-year-old will be confused by; the counting/light lesson is trivial.

j.learned_fact: Plants need sun and water to grow, and growth happens slowly over days.
j.thinking_skill: observes a change over time after acting on it (watering daily)
j.notes: The plot does not hold together: the leaf growing bigger would not stop Brooks from biting it, the monkey picture is a random insert, and the synagogue setting is decorative rather than used.

j.learned_fact: Cookies are made by mixing flour, butter and sugar, then baking in a hot oven until golden brown.
j.thinking_skill: follows a sequence of steps and waits for a result
j.notes: The crayon drawing is a bolted-on activity that never connects to the baking; 'poured the mix into a pan' is wrong for cookie dough and the ending arrives without any small problem or discovery.

j.learned_fact: You can find your way with a map by matching a marked landmark (the big tree with a red dot) to the real thing on the ground and then following the path between landmarks.
j.thinking_skill: matches symbols on a representation to real objects to plan a route
j.notes: The story is two unrelated halves: a map-reading lesson delivered as a First/Next/Then/Last checklist, followed by Owen suddenly performing guitar for a crowd; 'fragile instruments' is forced vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: On a map, blue lines are rivers and green areas are forests; rivers flow toward the ocean. (Brown as 'rocky places with stones' is a simplification; brown usually shows mountains or high ground.)
j.thinking_skill: notices a pattern across map features and uses it to locate a place
j.notes: Sentences like 'A pattern was forming in her mind, like puzzle pieces fitting together' and the ordinal-word scaffolding (first/next/then/last) are above a 7-year-old's natural register, and the 'discovery' is hollow because she finds the school by its red dot, not by the pattern.

j.learned_fact: You can measure a distance by counting steps, and repeating the same measurement on another day gives about the same number, so the measurement can be trusted.
j.thinking_skill: repeats a measurement to check that it is consistent
j.notes: Audrey 'found a stick' that is never used, and one hundred steps around an entire park is implausible; the story is thin but the repeat-to-verify idea is genuinely age-appropriate.

j.learned_fact: Water left in an open container in warm sunlight slowly disappears because it evaporates into the air; also, a story, an advertisement and a data chart serve different purposes (entertain, persuade, inform).
j.thinking_skill: infers an unseen cause (evaporation) from evidence gathered over several days
j.notes: Two curriculum objectives (text genres and evaporation) are stapled together with only a forced last-paragraph link; 'pleasant to wear' and 'a small pulse of steam' are awkward, and the ad paragraph ('didn't show real boots that real children could buy') is muddled.

j.learned_fact: None reliable. The closing observation is false as written: Parker's two halves 'looked the same size as Sofia's two halves, even though his whole apple had been bigger' cannot be true, since half of a bigger apple is bigger than half of a smaller one. Counting family members (4 vs 5) is far below 3rd-grade level.
j.thinking_skill: compares two quantities and notices one is greater by one
j.notes: The math content (counting to five, cutting an apple in half) is kindergarten level for an 8-year-old, and the one attempted insight about halves is wrong; 'delicious' and 'with humor in her voice' are forced word insertions.

j.learned_fact: Fast, upbeat music tends to make people feel energized and slow music tends to make them feel calm, so the same song can suit one person's mood and not another's.
j.thinking_skill: notices that preferences correlate with mood and designs a rule to satisfy two people
j.notes: Little is learned beyond a mood/tempo observation; the opening sentence about a creature that 'definitely did not dance' is a clumsy detour and the resolution is a bit too tidy.

j.learned_fact: Motor skills (drawing, knitting, game controls) improve through repeated practice because the hands learn coordination that the eyes alone cannot supply; the first attempts will not match what you picture.
j.thinking_skill: draws an analogy between two skills (video-game control and drawing) to explain learning
j.notes: Reads two grades younger than an 11-year-old in vocabulary and theme; 'notorious dragon' is a misused inserted word, and the grandmother's lesson is stated more than dramatized.

j.learned_fact: A cup of flour packed hard into the measuring cup holds much more flour than a cup scooped gently and leveled with a knife, so recipe amounts depend on measuring technique; creaming butter and sugar turns the mix pale and fluffy.
j.thinking_skill: tests a variable (scooping method) by direct side-by-side comparison
j.notes: For a 13-year-old the topic and prose are young (upper-elementary), 'the climax came when she pulled them out' is a jarring inserted word, and the ending over-explains the lesson.

j.learned_fact: A pendulum's period depends on its length (shorter swings faster, longer swings slower), and not on how far you pull it back. (Slight inaccuracy: a near-horizontal release does lengthen the period noticeably; the rule holds well only for small swings.)
j.thinking_skill: tests a variable, then rules out a competing variable (amplitude) with a control
j.notes: The observations contradict themselves ('almost exactly the same time' then 'No, wait'), the brother calls the short pendulum broken because it barely moves while the worker says it never stops swinging, and 'plague of hypnotic metallic snakes', 'excavate the problem' and 'extravagant test' are forced vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: Selective breeding: saving seeds only from the sweetest tomato plants year after year makes sweetness a stable trait in that line, and the selection must be repeated or the trait drifts. (The drift claim is overstated for mostly self-pollinating tomatoes, but the principle is sound.)
j.thinking_skill: generalizes a mechanism (repeated selection maintains a trait) and applies it to a new question
j.notes: Reads like a middle-school story for a 9th grader; 'synthesis' and 'redemption of his resistance' are shoehorned, and the cooking-demonstration analogy to genetics is vague and does not actually illuminate inheritance.

j.learned_fact: To find a bug, change just one thing and see what breaks; if the tax part is right after simplifying the tip, the error must be in the tip calculation.
j.thinking_skill: isolates a bug by changing one variable at a time
j.notes: The second half collapses into a rambling coffee-shop tangent stuffed with misused vocabulary ('predecessor model', 'It might seem ethical', 'commemorate their shift'); the debugging first half is fine but generic.

j.learned_fact: A controlled experiment changes one variable at a time (cold vs room-temperature eggs) and is repeated to confirm; room-temperature eggs blend better into batter. (The enzyme explanation the character reaches for is not why egg temperature matters in baking; the real reason is emulsification and even mixing.)
j.thinking_skill: designs a controlled experiment isolating one variable and replicates it
j.notes: The failure symptoms shift (rock-hard, cakey, dense, bitter, gummy) and are exaggerated for an egg-temperature change; 'fathom', 'discrepancy' and 'apathetic expression' are visibly inserted, and a bakery competition judged in a school gym is muddled.

j.learned_fact: When debugging, trace what the program actually does step by step; the bug may be in an early filter or setup rule you assumed was fine (a minimum-length filter of five characters silently dropped all three-letter names).
j.thinking_skill: identifies a hidden assumption and transfers the insight to a different problem
j.notes: The lesson is demonstrated well but then spelled out twice (Marcus's speech and the closing note-to-self); 'relegated', 'heresy' and 'vehement' are forced, and a sorted-list bug 'skipping every third entry' does not match a length filter.

j.learned_fact: Two honest studies can contradict because they measure different things: a lab test of a pesticide's breakdown in sterile soil under controlled conditions answers a narrower question than sampling real well water, and neither alone settles the real-world risk. Ask what a study measured before asking who funded it.
j.thinking_skill: distinguishes what each study actually measured and evaluates evidence against the question that matters
j.notes: 'An innocuous fact' and 'legitimized' are slightly off-register insertions, and the grocery-store coda is a touch pat; otherwise this is the strongest piece in the set.

j.learned_fact: In the coffee supply chain the farmer receives a very small share (illustrated as about 3% margin) because they have no leverage over middlemen; interventions like fair trade or price regulation shift costs and demand elsewhere, so you must ask how you would measure whether the system actually changed.
j.thinking_skill: asks how an intervention's success could be measured and traces second-order effects through a system
j.notes: 'Promulgate' and 'disparate' are inserted rather than natural, the margin figures are illustrative rather than sourced, and the ending is an easy gesture; the discussion itself is strong.

j.learned_fact: Meaning in a collage (and in language) arises from the relationship between elements and the viewer's act of looking, not from any single image or word alone; juxtaposition creates meaning neither part contained.
j.thinking_skill: tests a hypothesis about meaning by removing deliberate intention, then reinterprets the result
j.notes: The experiment is self-contradictory ('selected images and words deliberately and pasted them without intention'), 'solvency', 'quiescent' and 'enthralling' are decorative insertions, and the insight is abstract enough that a reader takes away a mood more than a usable idea.

j.learned_fact: A computer follows instructions exactly and cannot guess intent; a missing colon after a for-loop breaks a Python program; error messages differ for spelling versus logic errors; hard-coding a value like the current year (1995) makes a program silently wrong once time passes.
j.thinking_skill: distinguishes syntax errors from logic errors and traces a stale assumption in old code
j.notes: Reads as a grade 9-10 story for a 12th-grade target; 'the mesmerize quality' is ungrammatical, 'specious' is misapplied, the immunology analogy adds nothing, and the leap from a hard-coded year to caring about history class is strained.

j.learned_fact: Every choice carries an opportunity cost: choosing to be present at one event means accepting the loss of the other, and you cannot know in advance whether you chose right.
j.thinking_skill: reflects on opportunity cost and accepts the consequences of a choice
j.notes: No concrete fact or skill is learned; 'diaphanous veil', 'commodify', 'peccadillo' and 'fervent' are conspicuously inserted, and 'breath visible as small clouds' inside a gymnasium is a false physical detail.
